screens.title: Core Network Infrastructure Services
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll build an operational understanding of three services every network engineer relies on: DHCP for automatic IP assignment, DNS for translating names to addresses, and NTP for synchronized time. You will learn what each service does, why accurate configuration matters for security and troubleshooting, and how to verify that devices are using the right servers. For example, DHCP without a default gateway stops clients from reaching other networks, DNS failures prevent hostname resolution, and unsynchronized clocks complicate event correlation during incident response. We will also walk through Cisco IOS command examples to create a DHCP pool, configure a DHCP relay using ip helper-address, turn on DNS resolution with ip domain-lookup and ip name-server, and point a device to NTP servers. Practical verification commands and common mistakes are included so you can confirm behavior and avoid conflicts like forgotten excluded-address ranges or blocked NTP UDP traffic. By the end you’ll be able to configure R1 to serve VLAN10, relay VLAN20 requests, resolve names via Google’s DNS, and synchronize time with public NTP servers, while understanding the risks of rogue DHCP and firewall blocks. Ready to explore the core topics and set up a reliable foundation for network services?

screens.title: DHCP fundamentals and a DHCP pool example
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol is a client-server protocol that gives devices the configuration they need to communicate on an IP network. At its core, DHCP provides an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, lease duration, and optional domain name. The most common Cisco implementation uses DHCP pools defined with ip dhcp pool, where you declare the network statement and options like default-router and dns-server. For example, a pool for VLAN10 might specify network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0, default-router 192.168.10.1, and dns-server entries. A best practice is to exclude static addresses using ip dhcp excluded-address so your router, servers, and reserved devices are not assigned by DHCP. A typical mistake is forgetting exclusion ranges which leads to IP conflicts when a server or router IP is handed out to a client. Concretely, when a laptop boots it sends a broadcast DHCPDISCOVER; a DHCP server replies with DHCPOFFER, and after request and acknowledgement the client has an IP for the lease duration. Remember to set a reasonable lease (for example, an eight-hour lease during the day) so IP reuse is efficient but not disruptive. Example configuration is shown in the code panel; practice by creating a VLAN-specific pool and verifying bindings to see assigned addresses. What static devices in your network will you exclude first to avoid conflicts?

keyIdea.title: DHCP pool essentials
keyIdea.text: Define network, default-router, dns-server, domain-name, lease time, and exclude static IPs to prevent conflicts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › DHCP fundamentals
DHCP: what it provides
DHCP automates address assignment and related options so clients can join the network without manual config.
  • IP address and subnet mask for network reachability.
  • Default gateway for inter-subnet communication.
  • DNS servers and domain-name for name resolution.
  • Lease duration to control address reuse and churn.
Example
A laptop gets an 8-hour lease and DNS entries so applications can reach servers by name.
Common mistake
Not excluding router and server IPs can cause IP conflicts when DHCP assigns those addresses to clients.
Key Takeaway

Always reserve or exclude static IPs before enabling a DHCP pool and choose a lease time appropriate to client mobility.

DHCP pool configuration (Cisco IOS)
ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.9
ip dhcp pool VLAN10_POOL
 network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 192.168.10.1
 dns-server 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
 domain-name cohortia.local
 lease 0 8 0
!
Verification
Use show ip dhcp binding and show ip dhcp pool to inspect active leases and pool usage.
Practice prompt
Create this pool, then reboot a test client and confirm it receives the expected default-router and DNS entries.

screens.title: DHCP relay and ip helper-address
screens.narratorSegment: When a DHCP server is not on the same broadcast domain as a client, routers can act as DHCP relay agents so clients still receive addresses. The relay listens for DHCP broadcast messages from clients and forwards them as unicast packets to a configured DHCP server using the ip helper-address command on the interface that connects to the client VLAN. A common usage is when VLAN20 clients send a DHCPDISCOVER; the router on that VLAN uses ip helper-address 172.16.1.50 to relay the request to a central server. The relay preserves key DHCP fields so the server can respond correctly, and when the server replies the router forwards the reply back as a broadcast to the client subnet. Misconfigurations include pointing to the wrong DHCP server IP, forgetting to configure helper on the correct interface, or allowing helper traffic to pass through misconfigured ACLs. In practice, test the relay by clearing bindings and observing DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPOFFER exchanges using logs or packet captures. Also be cautious about trusting DHCP servers — a rogue DHCP server can hand out bad gateway or DNS values. After you configure helper-address, verify operation with show ip interface brief for the interface state and check the DHCP server logs or show ip dhcp binding to confirm leases are received from relayed clients. How will you validate that relayed clients receive the intended options?

keyIdea.text: Use ip helper-address on the client-facing interface to forward DHCP broadcasts to a remote DHCP server; verify with DHCP bindings and server logs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › DHCP relay
How DHCP relay works
A concise four-step process describing a client's request being forwarded and answered by a remote server.
1
Client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER
Client uses broadcast because it doesn't yet have an IP; router receives the broadcast.
2
Router forwards as unicast to DHCP server
ip helper-address converts broadcast to unicast and forwards to configured server IP.
3
Server replies with DHCPOFFER
The server selects an IP from its pool and sends an offer to the relay agent.
4
Router forwards offer to client and finalizes lease
Client completes the DHCP handshake and receives assigned options.
Config example
interface GigabitEthernet0/1 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0 ip helper-address 172.16.1.50 no shutdown
Example scenario
VLAN20 clients use R1 as relay to reach a central DHCP server at 172.16.1.50. After configuring helper-address, check server logs or show ip dhcp binding to confirm leases from VLAN20.
Common mistake
Applying helper-address to the wrong interface or using the wrong server IP prevents clients from ever reaching the DHCP server.
Verification
Use show ip interface brief to confirm the interface is up, and monitor the DHCP server for requests or use show ip dhcp binding to see relayed leases.

screens.title: DNS on Cisco devices
screens.narratorSegment: Domain Name System is the network service that translates human-friendly names into IP addresses so devices and administrators do not need to remember numeric addresses. On Cisco devices, resolution must be enabled with ip domain-lookup, and you provide name servers with ip name-server entries. The ip domain-name command appends a default domain to unqualified names and can help simplify lookups in a private network. A typical configuration uses public DNS servers such as 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4 for resolution, but internal name servers are common in enterprise environments. When DNS fails, devices cannot resolve hostnames used in logs, SNMP traps, or user commands like ping hostname, which hampers troubleshooting. Troubleshoot by checking show hosts for static entries, show ip name-server to confirm configured servers, and verifying connectivity to the DNS IP addresses. A common misconception is that adding ip name-server alone is enough; ip domain-lookup must be enabled so the device attempts DNS resolution. Also ensure that firewall rules allow DNS UDP and TCP port 53 between the router and its configured name servers. Practice: configure ip domain-lookup and ip name-server, then use ping with a known hostname and confirm resolution. How would you validate that the device is using the expected DNS server?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › DNS Configuration
DNS: purpose and configuration
DNS maps names to IPs; Cisco IOS requires enabling lookups and pointing to name servers.
ip domain-lookup
ip domain-name cohortia.local
ip name-server 8.8.8.8
ip name-server 8.8.4.4
Troubleshoot
  • show ip name-server — confirm server IPs.
  • show hosts — check static host entries.
  • Ping the DNS server to verify reachability.
Practice
After configuration, ping a known hostname and confirm an IP is returned so name-based tools work.
Example: reasoning
If logging shows hostnames but a device can’t ping those names, DNS resolution on the device is likely disabled or unreachable. Enabling domain-lookup and pointing to reachable name servers will restore name resolution.
Common misconception
Assuming DNS problems are application-layer only — in many cases the network device itself cannot resolve hostnames because ip domain-lookup is disabled or DNS servers are unreachable.

screens.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP)
screens.narratorSegment: Network Time Protocol keeps device clocks aligned across an infrastructure. Accurate time is essential for correlated logs, security protocols like certificate validation, and auditing. NTP uses a hierarchical stratum model: stratum 0 are reference clocks, stratum 1 servers sync to those, and stratum 2 servers sync to stratum 1, and so on. On Cisco devices you configure external time sources with ntp server commands and may mark one server as preferred. When no external source is available you can configure ntp master with a safe stratum, but this is a fallback and not a substitute for stable external servers. Misconfigurations often include pointing to incorrect IPs, firewall rules blocking UDP port 123, or setting an inappropriate stratum for a master which can confuse client selection. For example, configuring ntp server 162.159.200.1 prefer and ntp server 162.159.200.123 gives the device two public sources and designates the first as preferred. Verify synchronization with show ntp status to confirm clock offset and stratum, and show ntp associations to inspect peers. If you see large offsets or unsynchronized status, check network reachability and UDP 123 flows. Practice by pointing a router to two reliable sources and confirming it reports a synchronized state. What would you do first if show ntp status reports unsynchronized?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › NTP Configuration
NTP: purpose & model
NTP ensures consistent timestamps across devices, enabling accurate logs, security checks, and auditing.
ntp server 162.159.200.1 prefer
ntp server 162.159.200.123
!
ntp master 8
Verification
Use show ntp status to check synchronization and the reported stratum and offset.
Common issue
Firewalls blocking UDP 123 or wrong server IPs are frequent causes of unsynchronized devices.
Example: deciding to use ntp master
If external NTP servers are temporarily unavailable, an internal device may be configured as ntp master with a high stratum to provide time to local devices until external sources are restored. Prefer external servers when possible.
Key Takeaway

Synchronized clocks are critical for security and troubleshooting; always confirm reachability to NTP servers and check show ntp status after configuration.

screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through a practical configuration for Router R1 that covers interface addressing, a DHCP pool for VLAN10, a DHCP relay for VLAN20, DNS resolution, and NTP servers.   Utilization: 1/254

screens.title: Client vs Server roles and relay behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the roles of client, server, and relay helps diagnose where a failure is occurring. A DHCP client initiates the process by broadcasting a request. The DHCP server holds pools and options and assigns addresses. A DHCP relay acts as an intermediary when the server is remote. Conceptually, the relay does not assign addresses; instead it forwards client broadcasts to the server and returns the server’s replies to the client network. In practice, this matters when troubleshooting: if the client sends a broadcast but the server never sees it, the issue is likely relay configuration, interface state, or network ACLs. If the server receives the request but never assigns an IP, inspect server pools and excluded-address ranges. Compare a local server scenario where the server and client are in the same VLAN — here broadcasts reach the server directly — versus a relayed scenario where you must ensure helper-address and routing to the DHCP server are correct. A common misconception is that relays modify offered options; relays forward the request but certain vendor-specific options might be added or preserved by the server based on relay information. To validate, use server-side logs and show ip dhcp binding on the router to confirm which clients have active leases. Which part of the chain will you check first when a client reports no IP?

narration.text: Understanding the roles of client, server, and relay helps diagnose where a failure is occurring. A DHCP client initiates the process by broadcasting a request. The DHCP server holds pools and options and assigns addresses. A DHCP relay acts as an intermediary when the server is remote. Conceptually, the relay does not assign addresses; instead it forwards client broadcasts to the server and returns the server’s replies to the client network. In practice, this matters when troubleshooting: if the client sends a broadcast but the server never sees it, the issue is likely relay configuration, interface state, or network ACLs. If the server receives the request but never assigns an IP, inspect server pools and excluded-address ranges. Compare a local server scenario where the server and client are in the same VLAN — here broadcasts reach the server directly — versus a relayed scenario where you must ensure helper-address and routing to the DHCP server are correct. DHCP Client
Broadcasts discover messages, requests options. If a client gets no IP, check local interface and VLAN membership first.
DHCP Server
Manages pools and options, uses excluded ranges, and responds with offers. Verify pool capacity and static reservations.

Diagnostic checklist
  • Can the client ping the router interface? If not, check VLAN and interface state.
  • Does the router reach the DHCP server IP? Test with ping and route checks.

screens.title: Show commands: interpreting outputs
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is as important as configuration. Familiarize yourself with key show commands and what their output tells you. show ip dhcp binding lists active leases with client MAC addresses and lease types, which helps confirm clients received addresses. show ip dhcp pool displays pool statistics and utilization so you can detect exhaustion. For DNS, show hosts reveals static host entries while show ip name-server lists configured servers. For NTP, show ntp status tells you if the clock is synchronized, the current stratum, and the offset. show ntp associations lists peer relationships and indicates which server is selected. Interpreting results is a skill: a large offset in show ntp status suggests network latency or unreachable preferred servers; unsynchronized status points to reachability or firewall issues on UDP 123. For DHCP, if show ip dhcp binding shows no entries for a subnet you expect, check that clients are actually sending requests, confirm helper-address presence when the server is remote, and ensure server-side pool configuration exists. Use these commands iteratively as you tweak settings and remember to check both the router and the DHCP server logs when possible. When you see unexpected results, ask: did the client, relay, or server stop the exchange?

screens.title: Troubleshooting common issues and hardening
screens.narratorSegment: This screen focuses on common configuration mistakes and how to mitigate them. One of the most damaging problems is a rogue DHCP server on a network: an unauthorized device handing out IPs and gateway/DNS options can divert traffic or intercept data. To mitigate, restrict DHCP server placement, use DHCP snooping where available, and limit management access to trusted hosts. Another frequent error is forgetting to configure ip dhcp excluded-address for static devices; if the router's IP or a server IP falls within the pool, clients may receive those addresses causing conflicts. Always plan pool ranges and excluded addresses before enabling service. For NTP, firewalls blocking UDP port 123 or incorrect server IPs are typical causes of unsynchronized clocks. When time is off, certificate-based services and log correlation break. A practical troubleshooting flow is: confirm interface and VLAN state, validate DNS/NTP server reachability with ping, inspect dhcp bindings and server logs, and check any ACLs or firewall rules. Document your expected server IPs and maintain a checklist for changes. Finally, assume the services are critical: back up configurations and monitor service health so issues are found before users do. Which of these mitigations will you apply in your next network audit?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build an operational understanding of three services every network engineer relies on: DHCP for automatic IP assignment, DNS for translating names to addresses, and NTP for synchronized time. You will learn what each service does, why accurate configuration matters for security and troubleshooting, and how to verify that devices are using the right servers. For example, DHCP without a default gateway stops clients from reaching other networks, DNS failures prevent hostname resolution, and unsynchronized clocks complicate event correlation during incident response. We will also walk through Cisco IOS command examples to create a DHCP pool, configure a DHCP relay using ip helper-address, turn on DNS resolution with ip domain-lookup and ip name-server, and point a device to NTP servers. Practical verification commands and common mistakes are included so you can confirm behavior and avoid conflicts like forgotten excluded-address ranges or blocked NTP UDP traffic. By the end you’ll be able to configure R1 to serve VLAN10, relay VLAN20 requests, resolve names via Google’s DNS, and synchronize time with public NTP servers, while understanding the risks of rogue DHCP and firewall blocks. Ready to explore the core topics and set up a reliable foundation for network services?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure and verify core network services on a Cisco router. First, you will configure DHCP pools and exclusions to provide automatic IPv4 addresses and avoid conflicts; you will also configure a DHCP relay so clients on other VLANs can reach a central DHCP server. Second, you will enable DNS resolution on the router, set ip name-server entries, and validate that hostnames resolve correctly. Third, you will configure NTP client commands and, when needed, set a device as an NTP master with an appropriate stratum. Fourth, you will use verification commands such as show ip dhcp binding, show hosts, show ip name-server, show ntp status, and show ntp associations to confirm operational state. Each objective includes a practical verification step so you can test your configuration. These skills matter because misconfigured DHCP can cause IP conflicts, missing default-router values block internet access, DNS failures break name-based tools, and unsynchronized clocks make log correlation unreliable. You’ll practice with example IOS snippets and troubleshooting checks to build confidence and avoid common mistakes.

In addition to configuration, this chapter emphasizes verification and common mistakes you will observe in real networks. You will practice show commands such as show ip dhcp binding to confirm leases, show ip dhcp pool to inspect utilization, show hosts and show ip name-server for DNS checks, and show ntp status and show ntp associations for time alignment. You will learn to spot common mistakes: forgetting to exclude static addresses in a DHCP pool leads to IP conflicts, missing default-router prevents client access beyond their subnet, ip helper-address misconfiguration stops relayed DHCP, and firewalls blocking UDP 123 can prevent NTP synchronization. You will also see how to prioritize NTP servers with prefer and when to use ntp master with an appropriate stratum number for internal resilience. Finally, the objectives include practical advice on trusting DHCP servers and preventing rogue servers, and verifying DNS reachability before relying on name-based tools. These skills will help you not only configure services but also harden and validate them under real-world conditions.

Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol is a client-server protocol that gives devices the configuration they need to communicate on an IP network. At its core, DHCP provides an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, lease duration, and optional domain name. The most common Cisco implementation uses DHCP pools defined with ip dhcp pool, where you declare the network statement and options like default-router and dns-server. For example, a pool for VLAN10 might specify network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0, default-router 192.168.10.1, and dns-server entries. A best practice is to exclude static addresses using ip dhcp excluded-address so your router, servers, and reserved devices are not assigned by DHCP. A typical mistake is forgetting exclusion ranges which leads to IP conflicts when a server or router IP is handed out to a client. Concretely, when a laptop boots it sends a broadcast DHCPDISCOVER; a DHCP server replies with DHCPOFFER, and after request and acknowledgement the client has an IP for the lease duration. Remember to set a reasonable lease (for example, an eight-hour lease during the day) so IP reuse is efficient but not disruptive. Example configuration is shown in the code panel; practice by creating a VLAN-specific pool and verifying bindings to see assigned addresses. What static devices in your network will you exclude first to avoid conflicts?

When a DHCP server is not on the same broadcast domain as a client, routers can act as DHCP relay agents so clients still receive addresses. The relay listens for DHCP broadcast messages from clients and forwards them as unicast packets to a configured DHCP server using the ip helper-address command on the interface that connects to the client VLAN. A common usage is when VLAN20 clients send a DHCPDISCOVER; the router on that VLAN uses ip helper-address 172.16.1.50 to relay the request to a central server. The relay preserves key DHCP fields so the server can respond correctly, and when the server replies the router forwards the reply back as a broadcast to the client subnet. Misconfigurations include pointing to the wrong DHCP server IP, forgetting to configure helper on the correct interface, or allowing helper traffic to pass through misconfigured ACLs. In practice, test the relay by clearing bindings and observing DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPOFFER exchanges using logs or packet captures. Also be cautious about trusting DHCP servers — a rogue DHCP server can hand out bad gateway or DNS values. After you configure helper-address, verify operation with show ip interface brief for the interface state and check the DHCP server logs or show ip dhcp binding to confirm leases are received from relayed clients. How will you validate that relayed clients receive the intended options?

Domain Name System is the network service that translates human-friendly names into IP addresses so devices and administrators do not need to remember numeric addresses. On Cisco devices, resolution must be enabled with ip domain-lookup, and you provide name servers with ip name-server entries. The ip domain-name command appends a default domain to unqualified names and can help simplify lookups in a private network. A typical configuration uses public DNS servers such as 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4 for resolution, but internal name servers are common in enterprise environments. When DNS fails, devices cannot resolve hostnames used in logs, SNMP traps, or user commands like ping hostname, which hampers troubleshooting. Troubleshoot by checking show hosts for static entries, show ip name-server to confirm configured servers, and verifying connectivity to the DNS IP addresses. A common misconception is that adding ip name-server alone is enough; ip domain-lookup must be enabled so the device attempts DNS resolution. Also ensure that firewall rules allow DNS UDP and TCP port 53 between the router and its configured name servers. Practice: configure ip domain-lookup and ip name-server, then use ping with a known hostname and confirm resolution. How would you validate that the device is using the expected DNS server?

Network Time Protocol keeps device clocks aligned across an infrastructure. Accurate time is essential for correlated logs, security protocols like certificate validation, and auditing. NTP uses a hierarchical stratum model: stratum 0 are reference clocks, stratum 1 servers sync to those, and stratum 2 servers sync to stratum 1, and so on. On Cisco devices you configure external time sources with ntp server commands and may mark one server as preferred. When no external source is available you can configure ntp master with a safe stratum, but this is a fallback and not a substitute for stable external servers. Misconfigurations often include pointing to incorrect IPs, firewall rules blocking UDP port 123, or setting an inappropriate stratum for a master which can confuse client selection. For example, configuring ntp server 162.159.200.1 prefer and ntp server 162.159.200.123 gives the device two public sources and designates the first as preferred. Verify synchronization with show ntp status to confirm clock offset and stratum, and show ntp associations to inspect peers. If you see large offsets or unsynchronized status, check network reachability and UDP 123 flows. Practice by pointing a router to two reliable sources and confirming it reports a synchronized state. What would you do first if show ntp status reports unsynchronized?

Now we'll walk through a practical configuration for Router R1 that covers interface addressing, a DHCP pool for VLAN10, a DHCP relay for VLAN20, DNS resolution, and NTP servers. Follow each configuration block and think about why each command is present. First, assign IP addresses to GigabitEthernet0/0 and 0/1. The relay uses ip helper-address on the interface that serves VLAN20 so requests reach the central DHCP server. Next, create the DHCP pool VLAN10_POOL and exclude the router and a small static range to protect servers. Enable ip domain-lookup, set ip name-server entries, and configure ip domain-name for local resolution. Finally, add ntp server entries to synchronize time. After configuration, use show ip dhcp binding and show ip dhcp pool to confirm leases, show hosts and show ip name-server for DNS, and show ntp status/associations for time. A key troubleshooting step is to verify interface states and reachability to remote servers before concluding a misconfiguration. As you type each command, imagine verifying the outcome with the corresponding show command shown in the output panel. If a client fails to obtain an IP, check excluded-address overlap, helper-address correctness, and server reachability. This walkthrough maps directly to the lab template you will practice.

Understanding the roles of client, server, and relay helps diagnose where a failure is occurring. A DHCP client initiates the process by broadcasting a request. The DHCP server holds pools and options and assigns addresses. A DHCP relay acts as an intermediary when the server is remote. Conceptually, the relay does not assign addresses; instead it forwards client broadcasts to the server and returns the server’s replies to the client network. In practice, this matters when troubleshooting: if the client sends a broadcast but the server never sees it, the issue is likely relay configuration, interface state, or network ACLs. If the server receives the request but never assigns an IP, inspect server pools and excluded-address ranges. Compare a local server scenario where the server and client are in the same VLAN — here broadcasts reach the server directly — versus a relayed scenario where you must ensure helper-address and routing to the DHCP server are correct. A common misconception is that relays modify offered options; relays forward the request but certain vendor-specific options might be added or preserved by the server based on relay information. To validate, use server-side logs and show ip dhcp binding on the router to confirm which clients have active leases. Which part of the chain will you check first when a client reports no IP?

For DNS, show hosts reveals static host entries while show ip name-server lists configured servers. For NTP, show ntp status tells you if the clock is synchronized, the current stratum, and the offset. show ntp associations lists peer relationships and indicates which server is selected. Interpreting results is a skill: a large offset in show ntp status suggests network latency or unreachable preferred servers; unsynchronized status points to reachability or firewall issues on UDP 123. One of the most damaging problems is a rogue DHCP server on a network: an unauthorized device handing out IPs and gateway/DNS options can divert traffic or intercept data. To mitigate, restrict DHCP server placement, use DHCP snooping where available, and limit management access to trusted hosts. Another frequent error is forgetting to configure ip dhcp excluded-address for static devices; if the router's IP or a server IP falls within the pool, clients may receive those addresses causing conflicts. Always plan pool ranges and excluded addresses before enabling service. For NTP, firewalls blocking UDP port 123 or incorrect server IPs are typical causes of unsynchronized clocks.
